questions.prompt: Using Alice, task A and Bob's project B, explain why checking the task row's owner is not enough authorization for a PATCH that moves a task.

keyPoints.text: Constraining the PATCH by task id and Alice's id correctly protects the task row itself.
It still lets Alice write a project she does not own.
keyPoints.quote: It still permits a bad relationship if it writes project B without checking who owns B.

keyPoints.text: Authorization is not one gate at the top of the handler.
keyPoints.quote: Authorization is therefore not a single check at the beginning of the request.

keyPoints.text: Every resource whose relationship changes needs its own check.
keyPoints.quote: It must cover every resource whose relationship the operation changes.

keyPoints.text: Validating the destination does not replace the task's own user constraint.
keyPoints.quote: validating the destination does not authorize editing somebody else's task

keyPoints.text: The concrete guard is a findFirst on the project id plus the caller's id before the write.

questions.prompt: What do the destination lookup's two predicates prove, why is a uniform not-found response used, and how does the omitted-versus-supplied distinction affect the PATCH guard?

keyPoints.text: The lookup combines the submitted project id with the authenticated user's id.
keyPoints.quote: the submitted project ID and the authenticated user's ID

keyPoints.text: A hit proves the relationship is allowed right now.
keyPoints.quote: A result proves the requested relationship is allowed at that moment.

keyPoints.text: Absent and out-of-scope look identical so the response does not leak which one applies.
keyPoints.quote: Returning the same not-found shape avoids revealing which explanation applies

keyPoints.text: Omitting projectId means the relationship is not being changed.
keyPoints.quote: Omitting `projectId` means this request does not change that relationship.

keyPoints.text: An empty string parses and is not the same as omission.
keyPoints.quote: so `""` parses successfully and is *not* omission

keyPoints.text: So the route tests presence, not truthiness.
Security must not rely on lucky type coercion.
keyPoints.quote: Authorization should never depend on favorable coercion.

questions.prompt: Lookup and write are two separate statements. Explain how the guide decides whether that time gap matters in this codebase and what mechanism it recommends.

keyPoints.text: The lookup and the write are not one atomic proof.
keyPoints.quote: lookup and write are two statements, not one atomic proof

keyPoints.text: Whether the gap matters depends on which concurrent writes actually exist.
keyPoints.quote: check the repository instead of guessing

keyPoints.text: Look at the writers: the project PATCH schema accepts only areaId, name and order, and settings import sets userId to the caller on every row it creates.
keyPoints.quote: The project PATCH schema allows only `areaId`, `name` and `order`

keyPoints.text: A project can disappear between lookup and create.
The interleaving yields an ugly error rather than a cross-user link.
keyPoints.quote: So in this codebase the interleaving produces an ugly error, not a cross-user relationship.

keyPoints.text: A composite foreign key or conditional insert is only needed if ownership transfer arrives.
keyPoints.quote: becomes necessary only if an ownership-transfer feature is added

keyPoints.text: Pick mechanisms from real invariants, not from faith in transactions.
keyPoints.quote: Choose the mechanism from an actual invariant and failure scenario
